Across all participants, multiple S1 and SPL metrics showed modest associations with MOT performance (r = 0.20-0.40). Within athlete subgroups, stronger and task-specific associations were observed, particularly in the SCP and IPS groups (r = 0.50-0.80). Conclusions These findings identify distinct structural and functional patterns predominantly involving S1 and SPL across different motor participation profiles, despite comparable overall physical activity levels among the athlete groups. Such parietal differences are accompanied by difficulty-dependent differences in visual tracking performance and heterogeneous brain-behavior associations. Together, the results highlight S1 and SPL as the parietal regions showing the most consistent differentiation across structural and functional measures in association with distinct motor participation profiles and visual tracking performance, and provide a focused empirical basis for future investigations into the sources of this heterogeneity.

item.title: Multivariate Prediction of White Matter BOLD Activity and Its Relationship to Marginal Connectivity.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Functional MRI studies have traditionally focused on gray matter, whereas white matter BOLD signals have often been treated as weak or artifactual. However, white matter BOLD fluctuations are robustly detectable and contain reproducible functional information, yet most gray-to-white matter analyses rely on only marginal functional connectivity, which cannot separate pairwise coupling from shared variance among distributed cortical systems. Here, we used a multivariate cortical prediction framework to test whether spontaneous white matter BOLD activity can be predicted from distributed cortical gray matter BOLD activity, and how this predictive structure relates to marginal connectivity. Resting-state fMRI data from 81 Human Connectome Project young adult participants were analyzed using a strict white matter mask with no overlap with cortical predictors. For each white matter voxel, time series from 400 cortical parcels were used to predict white matter BOLD signals with nested leave-one-run-out ridge regression. Cortical BOLD activity modestly but reliably predicted white matter BOLD dynamics, demonstrating consistent cross-validated prediction accuracy across a broad spatial extent of the white matter. Ridge β coefficients strongly recapitulated marginal functional connectivity fingerprints, indicating a shared functional backbone, but their first gradients differed reproducibly. The difference between these gradients defined a β-minus-FC G1 divergence axis that remained stable after broadly controlling for anatomical, signal-related, and spatial factors. At the low end of the axis, enriched in callosal and capsular structures, pairwise gray-to-white matter connectivity was relatively strong, but white matter BOLD fluctuations were predicted less well by distributed cortical BOLD activity than that connectivity would suggest. At the high end, enriched in posterior projection and association pathways, pairwise connectivity was relatively weak, but distributed cortical BOLD activity predicted white matter BOLD signals better than expected. These findings identify a reproducible, tract-organized contrast between marginal connectivity and its covariance-adjusted predictive representation.

item.title: Functional connectivity and treatment response in obesity and eating disorders: Current evidence and empirical data.
item.description:
Reviews in endocrine & metabolic disorders
Alterations in large-scale brain networks have been reported in obesity (OB) and eating disorders (ED), but their relevance to treatment outcomes remains unclear. We reviewed evidence on neurobiological predictors of treatment outcome in ED and OB and present preliminary empirical analyses exploring baseline rsFC differences between individuals with anorexia nervosa (AN), obesity with comorbid ED (OB + ED), and obesity without ED (OB - ED) and healthy controls (HC), and examining whether these connectivity differences are associated with treatment outcome in the clinical groups. A total of 98 women (AN = 27, OB + ED = 25, OB - ED = 21, HC = 25) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). rsFC networks were subsequently identified using probabilistic independent component analysis (ICA), and their associations with treatment outcomes were examined within each clinical group. Both OB groups showed reduced rsFC relative to HC within a thalamic-basal ganglia network, specifically in a cluster located in the left inferior occipital cortex encompassing extrastriate visual regions. Baseline connectivity in this occipital cluster showed a positive, although non-significant, association with treatment outcome in the OB - ED group, whereas no significant associations were observed in AN or OB + ED. Given the non-significant nature of this exploratory association, the observed relationship should be considered hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in adequately powered samples. Further work is needed to clarify the role of sensory-integrative networks in treatment response across extreme weight conditions.

item.title: Symptom-related damage patterns in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective This study was undertaken to elucidate the neuroanatomical and network substrates underlying diverse seizure symptoms in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis (mTLE-HS) by applying multivariate support vector regression (SVR) to individualized structural symptom mapping and atrophy network mapping (ANM). Methods We retrospectively enrolled 216 patients with mTLE-HS and 460 healthy controls. Six non-mutually exclusive seizure symptoms were assessed. We performed left-right flipping of all images of right-sided mTLE-HS patients along the midline before processing the data. Individual atrophy gray matter maps were derived using normative modeling. Structural symptom mapping was performed using multivariate SVR lesion-symptom mapping. For each patient, indirect ANM maps were generated using a normative functional connectome and direct ANM maps using the patient's own resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Correspondence between the two ANM approaches was assessed using individual-level whole-brain spatial correlations of unthresholded maps and group-level Dice coefficients of thresholded maps. Results Individual structural atrophy patterns were spatially heterogeneous, whereas different seizure manifestations were associated with partially distinct structural patterns and more spatially convergent network-level associations. Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures were associated with thalamic network involvement, gestural/limb automatisms with anterior cingulate-related networks, ictal vocalization symptoms with perisylvian language networks, dysmnesia with hippocampal-posteromedial networks, emotional phenomena with prefrontal-temporal networks, and autonomic phenomena with medial prefrontal and limbic networks. Furthermore, limited spatial correspondence was observed between the results of the direct and indirect atrophy network analyses, suggesting the indirect and direct ANM can be regarded as nonequivalent but potentially complementary approaches. Significance In mTLE-HS, heterogeneous seizure manifestations are associated with distinct patterns of atrophy and distributed functional network involvement. ANM provides a complementary framework for characterizing symptom-related network patterns, and differences between indirect/normative and direct/patient-specific connectome analyses may provide complementary information.

item.title: The ovarian cycle and estradiol modulate cortical network state and auditory entrainment in mice and women
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
ABSTRACT The human brain is remarkably dynamic, continuously adapting to internal and external signals across rapid and protracted timescales. While both male and female brains are influenced by sex hormones to drive adaptive behavioural and physiological changes, the ovarian cycle in female mammals represents a conserved naturalistic model to understand how hormones such as estradiol (E2) alter cellular and network states to shape brain function. To understand whether and how the ovarian cycle influences sensory cortical processing, we investigated cortical network activity at rest and upon auditory stimulation across the ovarian cycle in mice and human subjects. We recorded EEG activity in men and women and intracortical local field potentials in male and female mice. Female participants were tested during two phases of their ovarian cycle characterized by low E2 levels (early follicular phase in women; late estrus in mice) and high E2 levels (late follicular phase in women; proestrus in mice). Across species, high endogenous or exogenous estradiol was associated with a steeper aperiodic power spectral slope, indicating decreased excitatory/inhibitory drive and attenuated auditory entrainment following a 40Hz stimulation. At the single-cell level, high E2 selectively increased the baseline and sustained 40-Hz firing of putative fast-spiking interneurons while reducing their temporal coherence during both spontaneous and stimulus-evoked activity, suggesting that E2 enhances inhibitory tone, while disrupting the temporal coordination of inhibitory networks. Altogether, these findings demonstrate that estradiol dynamically modulates cortical network states and auditory responsiveness. This underscores the necessity of investigating hormone-brain coupling as an evolutionarily conserved model essential for yielding translational insights into sex-specific neurobiology.

item.title: Adolescent prodromal phenotypes of psychiatric disorders: insights from a novel DISC1-perturbed monkey model
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
ABSTRACT Neurodevelopmental deficits frequently lead to mild but significant adolescent social and cognitive changes, representing prodromal manifestations of adult-onset psychiatric disorders in a cross-disease manner. Although experimental medicine utilizes animal models to address the mechanisms, rodent brains lack critical structures for human higher brain functions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. To fill this translational gap, we generated monkeys with an impaired DISC1 gene locus, targeting the multifunctional protein essential for neurodevelopment and involved in transdiagnostic mental health risks. Here we analyze the F0 animals by minimizing mosaicism. At ages equivalent to human adolescence, these monkeys exhibited blunted responsiveness to social stimuli and increased internal drives, mirroring altered social behaviors in the prodromal stage in humans. Resting-state functional MRI data indicated disrupted global functional connectivity and reorganization of network topology, marked by a shift in the dominance of brain hubs from prefrontal regions to sensory areas. This primate model provides a unique platform for studying psychiatric disorders, such as schizophrenia, across the developmental trajectory.

item.title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human.

item.title: Behavioral and neural modulation effects of transcranial pulse stimulation of the dorsal cingulate cortex and anterior insula cortex in healthy adults: A prospective, randomized, sham-controlled trial
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Transcranial pulse stimulation (TPS) is a novel non-invasive brain stimulation technique with promising neuromodulation effects. No studies have examined target-specific deep brain TPS. This study assessed whether TPS of the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and anterior insular cortex (AIC) modulates risk-taking behavior and brain circuits in healthy participants. Methods Seventy-five healthy adults were randomized in this subjects/raters-blind study to 10 sessions of active dACC-TPS, active AIC-TPS, or sham-TPS over 2 weeks. Balloon Analog Risk Task (BART), a psychological measure of risk-taking behavior with high ecological validity, was assessed at baseline, midpoint (Week 1), and endpoint (Week 2). Resting-state functional connectivity (rsFC) was measured at baseline and endpoint. Results Most participants experienced mild-to-moderate adverse events, primarily tingling and pain at the stimulation site. The overall dropout rate was 4%. Significant interactions emerged in the BART: dACC-TPS significantly decreased average pumps (average pumps on all trials), AIC-TPS significantly increased adjusted average pumps (average pumps on trials where the balloon did not burst), and sham showed no change. Target-specific rsFC changes were observed following active stimulation versus sham: dACC-TPS predominantly enhanced rsFC of dACC and AIC with precuneus, parietal, and occipital cortices, whereas AIC-TPS decreased rsFC of AIC with striatum. Conclusions Ten sessions of dACC-TPS and AIC-TPS are feasible and safe. dACC-TPS decreased risk-taking behavior, whereas AIC-TPS increased it. Bidirectional, target-specific rsFC changes were observed. Future large-scale studies with online neuroimaging or neurophysiological investigations are needed to confirm short- and long-term efficacy and clarify underlying mechanisms. Trial Registration ClinicalTrial.gov Identifier NCT06635161.

item.title: Altered intrinsic neural timescales in cocaine use disorder.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
Cocaine use disorder (CUD) is a major public health challenge, but its neurodynamic and molecular mechanisms remain unclear despite evidence of structural and functional abnormalities. This study mapped whole-brain intrinsic neural timescales (INTs), reflecting temporal integration of neural activity, using resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging in 44 CUD patients and 44 healthy controls. In the primary analysis with global signal regression (GSR), CUD showed increased network-level INTs in the visual, somatomotor, dorsal attention, frontoparietal control, and default mode networks compared with HC. In the sensitivity analysis without GSR, the visual and somatomotor network differences remained significant. Within the CUD group, regional and network-level INT variation was associated with individual differences in flanker-task performance, despite the absence of significant between-group differences in behavioral performance. Notably, the spatial distribution of INT differences was associated with normative maps of gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptors and the noradrenaline transporter. Atlas-based models showed modest discrimination and limited validation, while outcome-informed cluster-based models yielded higher but exploratory estimates. Importantly, classification performance in a mixed-source evaluation sample was close to chance, indicating limited generalizability. Together, these findings reveal widespread alterations in intrinsic neural timescales in CUD and highlight the relevance of spatiotemporal brain organization to addiction.

item.title: CAG repeat length shapes bidirectional functional connectome alterations in spinocerebellar ataxia type 3: a multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
Neuroscience
The ATXN3 gene is the primary driver of brain damage in spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3). We aimed to elucidate the patterns of connectome alterations shaped by cytosine-adenine-guanine (CAG) repeat length in SCA3. Eighty-nine genetically confirmed patients with SCA3 and 89 age-, sex-, education-matched healthy controls underwent multimodal MRI and comprehensive clinical assessments. Connectome-based predictive modeling (CPM) was used to identify functional connectivity patterns associated with CAG repeat length. Structural brain damage was assessed using voxel-based morphometry. Mediation analysis was performed to examine the role of structural impairment in connectivity changes. CPM identified a positive and a negative network, whose connectivity strength increased or decreased with CAG repeat length. The positive network (r = 0.397, P < 0.001) was mainly localized within the cerebello-motor circuit and was positively associated with ataxia severity and functional disability. The negative network (r = 0.243, P = 0.022) was distributed across large-scale networks, with selective vulnerability of interhemispheric connectivity, and was associated with motor dysfunction. Besides the canonical motor pathways, limbic-related connectivity was related to motor impairment. Structural analyses revealed widespread gray matter atrophy centered on the cerebellum. Cerebellar atrophy statistically mediated the association between CAG repeat length and connectivity decreases. CAG repeat length is associated with a bidirectional connectopathy in SCA3. Cerebellar atrophy may mediate the connectivity decreases. Future longitudinal studies are required to examine the underlying causal pathway.

item.title: Brain-thought states during movie-watching reflect shared sensory anchors and film- and person- specific processes in association cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Naturalistic paradigms such as movie-watching have transformed functional neuroimaging by capturing cognitive dynamics during rich, real-world experiences. A fundamental challenge, however, is determining whether the neural signatures identified during these experiences reflect general principles of cognition or the specific contexts in which they are measured. To address this question, we combined fMRI data from participants watching eight diverse films with continuous reports of ongoing thought. We found that the generalizability of brain-thought relationships depends on the cognitive process being recruited. Neural signatures linked to sensory processing remained robust across films, whereas those involving memory-related association networks depended on how we modelled between-film variability, indicating that cognition becomes increasingly context-dependent along the cortical hierarchy from sensory to association cortex. Within default and limbic networks, we identified two contrasting memory-related states with opposite consequences for comprehension. One, reflecting the integration of prior knowledge with ongoing experience, predicted better narrative comprehension and was revealed only after accounting for between-film variability. The other, associated with stimulus-independent thought, predicted poorer comprehension and emerged only when between-film variability was not modelled. Together, these findings establish when brain-experience relationships measured during naturalistic paradigms can generalize across contexts and when they instead reflect interactions between cognition and the specific environments in which cognition unfolds. More broadly, the consistency of a given brain-experiential association may depend less on where it occurs in the brain and more on the viewer’s contextual experience: perceiving the film, drawing on memory to understand it, or drifting away. Significance statement Films have revolutionized how we study healthy and atypical brain activity by capturing synchronized, semi-unconstrained dynamics of real-world cognition. Yet experience is rarely measured alongside brain activity, and most studies use one or few films; thus, we do not know whether these neural and experiential responses generalize across films. By combining brain imaging with continuous reports of ongoing thought, we find a hierarchy: sensory processing is consistent across films, whereas memory-related processes in association cortex are uniquely sensitive to how film context is modelled. Two opposing memory states relate to comprehension. One draws on memory to support understanding; the other reflects stimulus-independent thought and impairs it. Identifying brain–experience relationships across films is crucial for developing and understanding naturalistic neuroscience.
